stem: A restaurant offers 8 appetizers, 12 entrees, and 5 desserts on its menu. If a customer randomly selects one item from the entire menu, what is the probability that the item is an entree?
explanation: The total number of menu items is 8 + 12 + 5 = 25. The probability of selecting an entree is \frac{12}{25}. The answer \frac{8}{25} results from selecting the appetizer count instead of the entree count. The answer \frac{5}{25} results from selecting the dessert count. The answer \frac{12}{20} results from incorrectly calculating the total as 20 by omitting one category.

stem: At a high school, 90 students belong to the art club, the debate club, or both. Of these students, 54 belong to the art club and 60 belong to the debate club. If a student is selected at random from those who belong to the art club, what is the probability that this student also belongs to the debate club? Express your answer as a fraction.
explanation: By the inclusion-exclusion principle, the number of students in both clubs is 54 + 60 - 90 = 24. Given that a student is in the art club (54 students), the conditional probability that this student is also in the debate club is \frac{24}{54} = \frac{4}{9}. A common error is dividing by the total 90 instead of conditioning on art club membership, yielding \frac{24}{90}. Another error is dividing by 60 (the debate club total) instead of 54. Forgetting to use inclusion-exclusion and using 60 as the overlap count would also produce an incorrect answer.

stem: A medical screening test for a certain condition has a 95% true positive rate (it correctly identifies 95% of people who have the condition) and a 92% true negative rate (it correctly identifies 92% of people who do not have the condition). In a population of 10{,}000 people, 200 have the condition. If a person selected at random from this population tests positive, what is the probability that the person actually has the condition?
explanation: Of the 200 people with the condition, 0.95 \times 200 = 190 test positive (true positives). Of the 9{,}800 without the condition, 0.08 \times 9{,}800 = 784 test positive (false positives). The total number of positive tests is 190 + 784 = 974. The probability that a person who tests positive actually has the condition is \frac{190}{974}. The answer \frac{190}{784} incorrectly divides true positives by false positives only, omitting the true positives from the denominator. The answer \frac{190}{200} gives the true positive rate itself rather than the predictive value. The answer \frac{784}{974} gives the proportion of false positives among all positives, which is the complement of the correct answer.

skill: Inference from Sample Statistics and Margin of Error
stem: A random sample of 400 customers at a shopping mall found that 68% were satisfied with the mall's facilities. The margin of error for this estimate is 4.6 percentage points. Which of the following is the best interpretation of this result?

options.text: Exactly 68% of all mall customers are satisfied with the facilities.
Between 63.4% and 72.6% of the sampled customers are satisfied with the facilities.
It is plausible that between 63.4% and 72.6% of all mall customers are satisfied with the facilities.
If another sample is taken, exactly 68% of those customers will also be satisfied.

explanation: A margin of error defines a confidence interval around the sample statistic that provides a plausible range for the population parameter. Adding and subtracting 4.6 from 68 gives the interval 63.4% to 72.6% for all mall customers. The answer stating exactly 68% treats the sample statistic as the exact population value, ignoring sampling variability. The answer referring to the sampled customers applies the interval to the sample rather than the population. The answer predicting the next sample will yield exactly 68% confuses a point estimate with a guaranteed replication.

skill: Inference from Sample Statistics and Margin of Error
stem: A weather service randomly selects 600 of its daily forecasts from the past year and finds that 78% were accurate. If the margin of error at the 95% confidence level is approximately \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} for a sample of size n, what is the approximate margin of error, to the nearest hundredth?
explanation: Using the given approximation, the margin of error is \frac{1}{\sqrt{600}}. Since \sqrt{600} \approx 24.49, this gives \frac{1}{24.49} \approx 0.0408, which rounds to 0.04 to the nearest hundredth. A common error is using n = 78 (the percentage) instead of n = 600 (the sample size). Another error is forgetting to take the square root and computing \frac{1}{600}. Computing \sqrt{600} incorrectly as 60 would yield \frac{1}{60} \approx 0.02.

skill: Inference from Sample Statistics and Margin of Error
stem: Two independent random samples are taken to estimate the proportion of residents in a city who support a new public transit plan. Sample 1 surveys 500 residents and finds 52% support, with a margin of error of 4.4 percentage points. Sample 2 surveys 1{,}200 residents and finds 46% support, with a margin of error of 2.8 percentage points. Based on these confidence intervals, which of the following conclusions is most justified?

options.text: A majority of all city residents support the plan, because Sample 1 found more than 50% support.
Fewer than half of all city residents support the plan, because Sample 2 has a larger sample size and is therefore more reliable.
The confidence intervals overlap, so the data do not provide strong evidence that the true proportion differs between the two samples.
The true proportion of residents who support the plan is exactly 49%, the average of the two sample proportions.

explanation: Sample 1 gives a confidence interval of (47.6%, 56.4%) and Sample 2 gives (43.2%, 48.8%). These intervals overlap in the range (47.6%, 48.8%), so the data do not provide strong evidence that the true population proportion is different between the two estimates. The conclusion that a majority supports the plan relies only on Sample 1 while ignoring Sample 2's contradictory result. The conclusion favoring Sample 2 solely because of its larger size ignores that the intervals overlap. Averaging the two sample proportions to obtain an exact value misrepresents how confidence intervals work and treats an estimate as a precise parameter.

skill: Evaluating Statistical Claims: Observational Studies and Experiments
stem: Researchers want to determine whether a new organic pesticide reduces crop damage compared to the standard pesticide. They randomly assign 40 identical plots to receive either the new organic pesticide or the standard pesticide. At the end of the growing season, they compare the average crop damage between the two groups. This study is best described as

options.text: a survey, because the researchers collected data from the plots.
an observational study, because the researchers observed crop damage.
an experiment, because the researchers randomly assigned treatments to plots.
a census, because the researchers examined all 40 plots.

explanation: The study is an experiment because the researchers actively imposed a treatment (type of pesticide) by randomly assigning plots to groups. Random assignment of treatments is the defining feature of an experiment. Calling it a survey is incorrect because surveys collect self-reported information from respondents, not measurements on experimental units. Calling it an observational study is incorrect because the researchers controlled which treatment each plot received rather than merely observing existing conditions. Calling it a census is incorrect because a census attempts to measure every member of a population, which is not the design here.

skill: Evaluating Statistical Claims: Observational Studies and Experiments
stem: A company randomly assigns $120$ employees to either a standing-desk group or a traditional-desk group to study the effect on daily productivity scores. After $8$ weeks, the standing-desk group has a significantly higher mean productivity score than the traditional-desk group. Which of the following conclusions is best supported by the design of this study?

options.text: Standing desks cause higher productivity scores among all office workers.
Standing desks cause higher productivity scores among the employees in this company.
There is an association between desk type and productivity scores among the employees in this company, but causation cannot be established.
The results can be generalized to all companies that use standing desks.

explanation: Because the study uses random assignment of treatments (standing desk vs. traditional desk) to the $120$ employees, it is a randomized experiment, which can support a causal conclusion. However, the participants are employees at one specific company, not a random sample of all office workers, so the causal conclusion applies only to this company's employees. The claim that standing desks cause higher productivity among all office workers overgeneralizes beyond the study population. The claim that only an association can be established incorrectly denies the causal inference that random assignment permits. The claim that results generalize to all companies ignores that the sample was drawn from a single company.

skill: Evaluating Statistical Claims: Observational Studies and Experiments
stem: A hospital conducted a study in which patients who chose to take a daily vitamin supplement were compared to patients who chose not to take the supplement. After one year, the supplement group had a lower rate of respiratory infections. A health magazine reported that taking the vitamin supplement reduces respiratory infections. Which of the following is the most significant flaw in the magazine's conclusion?

options.text: The study did not include a placebo group.
Because patients chose whether to take the supplement, the groups may differ in health-conscious behaviors that also affect infection rates, so a causal conclusion is not justified.
The study lasted only one year, which is too short to draw any conclusions.
The sample size of the study was not reported in the magazine article.

explanation: The most significant flaw is that this is an observational study, not an experiment: patients self-selected into groups. People who choose to take supplements may also exercise more, eat healthier, or engage in other behaviors that reduce infection risk. These confounding variables make it impossible to attribute the lower infection rate to the supplement alone. While the absence of a placebo group is a limitation, the fundamental problem is the lack of random assignment, not just the absence of a placebo. The one-year duration, though potentially a concern, does not address the core issue of confounding. The unreported sample size is a reporting deficiency but does not explain why the causal claim is unjustified.
